summary: This Dockerfile creates a Ubuntu container with zsh, ripgrep, fzf, and bat pre-installed, then sets up a custom zsh function called `rgf` that lets you interactively search code and open results in VSCode. It also creates a demo project directory with sample code files containing various issues (secrets, TODOs, hardcoded ports) that the rgf function is designed to find.

explanations.3: This environment variable tells the Ubuntu package installer to run non-interactively, so it won't prompt you for input during installation in the container.
explanations.7: Ubuntu's default package repositories only include 'main' and 'restricted' software; this command adds 'universe' and 'multiverse' so we can install fzf and bat, which live in those sections.
explanations.15: After installing packages, we delete the apt package cache to reduce the final image size, since we won't need to install anything else.
explanations.22: The `printf` command with `%s\n` is being used to write multiple lines of a zsh shell script; each quoted string becomes one line in the output.
explanations.32: This runs the `uname -s` command to detect the operating system type (Darwin for macOS, Linux for Linux, etc.) so the error messages can suggest the right install command.
explanations.34: The `command -v` utility checks if a program exists in the PATH; the `>/dev/null 2>&1` part silently discards both standard output and error messages.
explanations.44: This checks if either `bat` or `batcat` is installed because Ubuntu/Debian systems rename the bat binary to `batcat` to avoid conflicts with another package.
explanations.72: This declares a local variable that will hold either 'bat' or 'batcat' depending on which one is available on the system.
explanations.83: This creates a temporary file with a unique name pattern; the script will write fzf's output there instead of using command substitution, which avoids issues in certain shells.
explanations.85: The `--color=always` flag tells ripgrep to include color codes in its output even though it's piped; this way the colors show up in the fzf preview.
explanations.89: The `--delimiter=':'` tells fzf that fields are separated by colons (the format ripgrep outputs is filename:linenumber:content).
explanations.90: The `--nth=3..` tells fzf to search starting from the third field onward (the actual file content), skipping the filename and line number.
explanations.91: This `--preview` option tells fzf what command to run when highlighting a result; it uses bat to show a preview of the file with that specific line highlighted.
explanations.96: This reads the selected line from the temporary file into the `selected` variable; `$(<"file")` is a bash/zsh shorthand for reading a file's contents.
explanations.100: This checks two exit conditions: either fzf exited with a non-zero code (user pressed Escape or Ctrl-C), or the selected string is empty, in which case we exit the function.
explanations.104: This extracts the filename (first field) from the selected line, first removing ANSI color codes using sed (the regex `\033\[[0-9;]*m` matches color escape sequences).
explanations.105: Similar to the previous line, this extracts the line number (second field) after stripping color codes.
explanations.115: The `> /root/.zsh/fns/rgf` redirects all the printf output to create the rgf script file; without a newline at the end, this overwrites the file.
explanations.120: The `>>` operator appends to the file instead of overwriting it, so we're adding the autoload configuration to the existing `.zshrc`.
explanations.126: This creates a `.env` file containing a deliberately exposed database password—a real-world example of a secret that the rgf function could help you find.
explanations.141: This adds a custom zsh prompt that displays a whale emoji and colored user/path info to make it visually obvious you're inside a container.
